WHY THIS HOUR MATTERS

Atlanta ranks last in upward mobility

The number behind the ranking

Opportunity Insights followed 57 million children born between 1978 and 1992. Among the fifty largest metro areas, Atlanta finished last for children raised in low-income families.

4.5% vs. 7.5%

The odds a child born in the bottom fifth here reaches the top fifth, against the national rate. In San Jose, it is 12.9%.

The degree is the equalizer

A bachelor's degree carries a median lifetime earnings premium of about $1.2 million — and at any given college, low-income graduates go on to earn roughly what everyone else does.

$2.8M vs. $1.6M

Median lifetime earnings, bachelor's degree against high school diploma.

The return is not automatic: more than a quarter of bachelor’s programs never pay back their cost once the risk of not finishing is counted. School, major, and completion are the decision.

PART 1 · THE GEORGIA LANDSCAPE

Four forces shaping the Class of 2027

HEADWIND

Test scores are required again

Georgia State, Kennesaw State, and Georgia Southern require an ACT or SAT for Fall 2026. GPA-only admission ends.

HEADWIND

Parent borrowing gets a ceiling

From July 2026, Parent PLUS is capped at $65,000 per student. Families who once borrowed full cost no longer can.

TAILWIND

The SAT college readiness bar is lowered

College Board's benchmark is 1010; an ACT of 21 concords to roughly 1080. Testing both can change the answer.

TAILWIND

DREAMS Scholarship launched

Georgia's first statewide need-based aid — up to $3,000 a year, with no application beyond the FAFSA.

HEADWIND · THE NEAR-TERM DEADLINE

Test scores are required again

Beginning Fall 2026, the University System of Georgia reinstates the ACT/SAT requirement for admission. For four years these were GPA-only admits. That door closes for the students sitting in this room.

WHAT CHANGED

The requirement is back

A test score is once again part of the admission file. Not optional, not a bonus — required.

WHERE IT BITES

Three familiar names

Georgia State, Kennesaw State, and Georgia Southern — among the most common destinations for Atlanta families.

WHAT TO DO

Register this week

Sit for a fall date early enough to retake once before applications are due. One attempt is rarely the best score.

SENIORS

Sit for a test this fall — including at test-optional schools. A score can only help: admission, scholarship eligibility, and Zell Miller, which requires one.

JUNIORS

Take the PSAT/NMSQT in October — the 11th-grade sitting is the only entry to National Merit. The PSAT 10 and PSAT 8/9 do not count, and scores also feed College Board's recognition awards.

TAILWINDS · WHERE THE LEVERAGE IS

Two openings worth acting on

Sit for both tests

College Board sets its college-readiness benchmark at 1010 — 480 on Reading and Writing plus 530 on Math. An ACT of 21 concords to roughly 1080, seventy points higher.

1010 vs. 1080

A student near the line can clear readiness on the SAT and miss it on the ACT. Take a diagnostic of each before committing.

Claim the DREAMS award

Georgia's first statewide need-based aid, and the counterpart to merit-based HOPE. There is no separate application — the FAFSA is the whole gate.

$3,000/yr × 8 semesters

Up to $12,000 across a four-year degree — for filing a form you were already asked to file

Bottom line: the testing requirement is the near-term deadline. DREAMS is money already on the table. The loan cap is the one to plan around.

PART 2 · PAYING FOR COLLEGE

What college actually costs

Cost of Attendance is the full number a school uses to build your aid package — not just the tuition line

DIRECT COSTS

Billed by the school

•Tuition

•Mandatory fees

•Housing

•Meal plan

+

INDIRECT COSTS

Real, but never on the bill

•Transportation and travel home

•Books and course materials

•Supplies, technology, personal expenses

Families budget for the bill and get blindsided by the rest. Plan for the whole Cost of Attendance.

PART 2 · PAYING FOR COLLEGE

The sticker price is not the price

What a college charges and what a family actually pays are two different numbers — and one policy decides the gap

MEETS FULL NEED, NO LOANS

The school covers the entire gap between Cost of Attendance and what the aid formula says the family can pay — with grants, not debt. Fewer than a hundred colleges do this.

MEETS FULL NEED, WITH LOANS

The gap is covered, but part of the package is a federal loan the student repays. Still a real offer — read the line items before you celebrate.

GAPPED

The package does not reach the full Cost of Attendance. Whatever is left is the family’s to find. Most colleges sit here.

Run the net price calculator, not the tuition page. Every college is required by law to publish one.

A private college with a $70,000 sticker can cost a low-income family less than a public one. Never cross a school off the list on the price tag alone.

Ask every admissions rep the same question: what percentage of demonstrated financial need does your school meet, and how much of that is loan?

PART 2 · PAYING FOR COLLEGE

Where the money comes from

FOUR SOURCES

Federal

State

Institutional

Independent

Aid is stackable — most students end up drawing from more than one of these.

FEDERAL AID AT A GLANCE

Pell Grant

$767 – $7,395

Need-based. Does not have to be repaid.

Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (FSEOG)

$100 – $4,000

Need-based, awarded by the school while funds last.

Direct Loans

5.50%

Subsidized and unsubsidized. Borrowed by the student.

Parent PLUS Loan

$65K cap

New lifetime limit per student ($20K/yr) from July 2026. 8.05%, credit-based.

Grants first, then scholarships, then loans. Always in that order.

PART 3 · SCHOLARSHIPS WORTH KNOWING

Where the big awards live

Cooke Young Scholars Program

Grade 7 · Jack Kent Cooke Foundation. Five years of advising and enrichment funding, 8th–12th grade. AGI under $95K; April deadline.

QuestBridge National College Match

Seniors · Full ride to partner colleges. Income under $65K, SAT 1260+ or ACT 27+, top 5-10% class rank.

5 Strong Scholarship

Seniors · Full tuition at partner HBCUs, paired with ongoing mentorship.

Common Black College Application

Seniors · One application, many HBCUs, one fee. We have a contact with the CEO about a future visit.

Local Atlanta sources

All ages · Community Foundation for Greater Atlanta, Divine 9 chapters, employer, alumni, and credit union awards.

Start earlier than feels necessary.

The largest awards in this list are decided years before senior year — and the local ones have the least competition.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

The vocabulary you'll need

Early Decision

Binding. If admitted, you attend and withdraw other applications.

Early Action

Non-binding. Apply early, hear early, decide in the spring.

Regular Decision

The standard deadline, typically January.

Rolling Admission

Reviewed as received. Applying early genuinely helps.

TEST-OPTIONAL vs. TEST-BLIND

Test-optional means a score is considered if you send it. Test-blind means it is not looked at all. The distinction matters, but the instruction does not change: every senior should still sit for the ACT. A score can only help — for admission, for scholarships, and for Zell Miller.

Before signing an ED agreement: be confident in the plan to pay. Favor schools that meet full demonstrated need — and know a family can withdraw an ED commitment if the aid package turns out to be unaffordable.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Demonstrated interest — the free lever

Open the emails they send

Many colleges track whether you open, click, and reply. It costs nothing, it takes seconds, and it is logged in your file.

Register for everything you attend

Fairs, rep visits, virtual sessions, tours — sign in every time with the same email you will apply with, or the visit does not count.

Ask a real question in writing

Email the admission counselor assigned to Georgia. Ask something the website does not answer. Sign your full name and high school.

Apply early rather than late

Applying in the early round is the strongest signal available — and for a family that cannot afford to travel, it is the cheapest one.

Write the supplement like you mean it

The "Why us?" essay is where interest gets graded. Name the program, the professor, the requirement — not the weather and the campus photos.

Not every college counts demonstrated interest, and the most selective often do not. But the schools most likely to hand your student money usually do.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Free ways to see a campus — and be seen

Fly-in programs

Seniors · Colleges cover airfare, room, and meals for first-generation and lower-income seniors. Caltech Up Close closes Aug 5, Access to Amherst Aug 10, Holy Cross Perspectives Sept 16.

Summer pre-college programs

Grades 10–11 · Selective universities run one- to three-week sessions and waive the fee for lower-income families. A few cover travel as well.

Virtual admission programs

Grades 9–12 · Multi-week online series run by admission offices that teach the process itself — essays, aid, strategy — not just the school.

Rep visits and college fairs

Grades 9–12 · Admission travel season runs August to early November. The rep who comes to Atlanta is usually the first person to read your student’s file.

Campus visits you can drive to

All ages · Register through the school’s own website so the visit goes on record. Georgia has dozens of campuses within a two-hour drive.

Every one of these is free.

They are also the cheapest way to show a college your student is serious — which at many schools is part of the decision.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Six questions before a school goes on the list

A ranking tells you what other people think. These tell you whether it works for your student.

Completion

Do students actually finish here?

Look up the six-year graduation rate before you fall in love with a campus.

Cost

What will this cost after aid?

Run the net price calculator on the school's own website. Every school has one.

Academics

Is my student inside the admitted range?

Compare GPA and test scores to the middle 50% the school publishes.

Career

Does this lead where my student wants to go?

Look for the major, the internships, and where graduates actually get hired.

Belonging

Will my student feel at home here?

Size, setting, distance from home, and who else is in the room all count.

Support

Who is in their corner once they arrive?

Ask about advising, tutoring, and first-generation programs on the visit.

A school that fails any one of these is not a good school for your student — no matter how good it looks on a list.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Apply at the level your student earned

The mistake has a name

Researchers call it undermatching: enrolling somewhere less selective than your record would have gotten you into. It happens at every income level, and it happens most to first-generation and low-income students.

Not a stretch — a fit

A student in the top 10% of their class who applies only to open-admission schools has undermatched. What is usually missing is information and confidence, not ability.

Why the level matters

Undermatched students finish college at lower rates than similar students who applied at their level. The more selective school is often the one with more aid, smaller classes, and more advising.

More aid, not less

The colleges with the largest endowments are frequently the cheapest for a low-income family after aid. Selectivity and affordability move together more often than families expect.

Bottom line: apply where the record says your student belongs. The worst outcome is not a rejection — it is never finding out.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Build a balanced list

Where a student applies matters as much as how well they apply

LIKELY

Admission is very probable given the student's GPA and scores. Do not treat these as consolation prizes.

TARGET

The student's profile sits squarely inside the school's admitted range. Most of the list belongs here.

REACH

Admission is possible but uncertain. Worth applying to — not worth building the plan around.

Eight to ten programs is a workable list, weighted toward likely and target.

At least one school on it must be affordable if no merit money comes through.

Where a student is ready and the school meets full need, applying early can meaningfully improve the odds — the most selective colleges fill a large share of the class in their early rounds.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Four ways into the essay

Two questions decide which one is yours: have you lived through something that changed you, and do you know what you want to study?

CHALLENGE · DIRECTION KNOWN

Draw the line between them

Tell what happened, what you did about it, and how it made you the person who belongs in that field.

NO BIG CHALLENGE · DIRECTION KNOWN

String the moments together

Pick one thread — food, repair, teaching — and show five small moments that built the person heading toward it.

CHALLENGE · DIRECTION OPEN

End on who you became

Same story, different landing. What you did and what it taught you is enough — no career has to be named.

NO BIG CHALLENGE · DIRECTION OPEN

Write what you love, closely

Start from one object, place, or obsession and go deep on specifics. Plenty of strong essays begin here.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Five things that make an essay work

Open in the middle of something

Skip the throat-clearing. Start where the story is already moving and let the reader catch up.

Sound like yourself out loud

If you would not say the sentence to a teacher you like, cut it. Thesaurus words read as borrowed.

Trade adjectives for specifics

Not "I love science." The smell of the lab at 6 a.m. and the experiment you ran four times.

Show the change, not just the event

The hard thing that happened matters less than what you now do differently because of it.

Get eyes on it early and often

A first draft in September beats a perfect draft in December. Read it aloud to someone who knows you.

The essay is the only part of the application where the reader hears your voice. Spend the time there.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

What actually counts as an activity

Colleges are not counting clubs. They are reading for depth, responsibility, and what a student did with the time they had.

Depth

Did you stay with it?

Four years of one thing reads stronger than one year of four things. Longevity is the easiest signal to see.

Responsibility

Were you the one counted on?

An officer title is one form of leadership. Opening the building, closing the register, and running the practice are others.

Family

Do you work or care for someone at home?

A job, a younger sibling, an ill parent — these belong on the application. They explain the schedule and they show the character.

Church

Does the ministry work count?

Yes. Usher board, praise team, youth ministry, VBS, and mission trips are activities with real hours and real leadership.

Initiative

Did you start or fix something?

A tutoring table, a food drive, a small business, a repair service. Scale matters less than the fact that it was yours.

Evidence

Can anyone verify it?

Keep hours, dates, roles, and a name who can confirm. A list written in April of senior year is a guess.

An activity list is a portrait, not an inventory. Five real things read stronger than twelve thin ones.

PART 4 · APPLYING WELL

Help the people writing your letters

A teacher or counselor writes from what is in front of them — give them more than a memory of your class participation

WHAT TO HAND THEM

Four weeks before the deadline

•A one-page brag sheet

•Your resume and activity list

•The colleges and majors on your list

•One story you want them to tell

+

WHAT ONLY THEY CAN SAY

The things your own essay cannot

•How you compare to the other students they teach

•What you took on when the school offered little

•Why a grade dipped the semester something happened at home

Ask in person, ask early, and follow up with a thank-you note. A rushed letter and a strong letter come from the same teacher.
